questions.explanation: The recovery without a restart is what makes this one condition rather than two. A nightly job that cannot write and a service that cannot write its own log entry are the same failure seen by two writers, and both began when the volume reached zero free space and both stopped when space was freed, with nothing else changed. The clean check on Friday evening is a control in time: with 3 percent used neither writer was failing, so the state that separates the two periods is the one the report tracks. A timeout establishes only that the waiting side stopped waiting, and the sender cannot know whether nothing was listening or something was and did not answer. questions.explanation: Readings taken along a route are cumulative, so each one is the sum of every section before it, and the only way to attribute the total is to difference the readings. Between the second and the third the time rises by 183 milliseconds, and between the third and the fourth by 2, so one section of the path carries almost the entire 189. The three wrong readings each pick a single printed number, which is the mistake this kind of table invites because the numbers look like measurements of places rather than of journeys. The largest reading is the largest by construction on any path, and the first two are small precisely because they were taken before the delay was accumulated.

questions.explanation: The steps are ordered by what each one would make the next one worth doing. The bound addresses come first because they can account for the entire pattern on their own: a socket on a local address answers the host and nobody else, and every later step is wasted effort if that is the answer. Rebinding is the natural response to that specific finding, and retesting from outside immediately confirms or refutes it. Only when the socket is already on the right address does the question become where an arriving request stops, and only when requests are arriving but going unanswered does a capture from a second machine have a boundary to place.

questions.explanation: The two conditions differ in exactly one respect that can be observed without help from anyone: a lock ends by itself after a stated interval, and an end date does not. So waiting is a diagnostic step, not a workaround, and the account's own record after the stated interval settles it in one reading. answer.exemplar: A timeout is a decision the waiting program made, and the number in the report is the length of the window it chose, not a measurement of the far end. When the program stops waiting it has learned exactly one thing, which is that nothing arrived inside its own patience, and every cause consistent with that produces the same line in the log. A service that has stopped, a service that is thinking, a segment lost in the middle of a path, a name that resolved to a host on the other side of the world, and a service answering from a queue forty requests deep are all silent for the whole of the window and all report the same elapsed figure to the millisecond. The number becomes informative in only one situation, and it is the situation the report cannot supply: when the far end timestamps its own work and the two figures are compared. Then a difference between them is real, but the single figure the waiting program holds is a statement about the reader, not about the thing being waited for.

questions.explanation: The figure in a timeout report is the length of a window the waiting program chose for itself, so it measures its own patience rather than the peer's performance and cannot distinguish a stopped service from a slow one.
questions.hint: Ask who chose the number, and what the program knew when it stopped waiting.
questions.learningObjective: explain why a timeout value says more about the waiting program than the peer

answer.exemplar: The value of a refusal is that it is an answer, and the value of silence is that it is not. A refusal has to be produced deliberately by something at the far end, because a segment lost in the middle of a path generates no reply from anyone: the device that discards it is not the destination and has no opinion about what was addressed there. So a refusal rules out the entire route, the address, and every remote cause in a single report, and leaves one narrow question: what is bound to that port on that host. A timeout leaves the same investigation with a list, because it is consistent with a refused connection, a lost segment, a service that is thinking, a name that resolved somewhere useless, and a service that is not running at all. The temptation to prefer the timeout report is that it sounds more serious, and it is worth naming that the order of usefulness here runs opposite to the order of alarm. The one thing a timeout can add is a bound on how long to keep waiting, and nothing about who is at fault.

questions.explanation: A refusal is a deliberate answer from the far end, so it eliminates the route, the address and every remote cause at once, while a timeout is equally consistent with all of them and narrows nothing.
questions.hint: Ask which of the two reports was produced on purpose by the far end.
questions.learningObjective: explain why a refusal narrows a failure more than silence does

answer.exemplar: A processor that is nearly idle under load is a measurement of the one resource that is not the problem, and it is the most useful number in the report for that reason. Capacity and latency are separate quantities: a service can be waiting a long time while the thing that does its arithmetic is almost entirely free, because the waiting is happening somewhere the processor never touches. What sits in that somewhere is usually the thing the service needs in order to answer, and it has a queue of its own that the report can often quantify directly, in the shape of a device that reports how much of an operation's time was spent waiting rather than working. Two habits work against reading this properly. The first treats a queue as a symptom of the processor, because queues are what saturated processors produce, when in fact a queue is what everything upstream of a constraint produces. The second assigns every delay to the program, on the grounds that a service must be responsible for its own slowness, which is a statement about where attention is usually directed rather than about where the time was spent.

questions.explanation: An idle processor removes the one resource that could be the constraint, so the delay has to be in a queue the processor never touches, and a device reporting that most of its time is spent waiting is that queue measured.
questions.hint: Ask which resource the idle figure has just cleared, and where the waiting can be if not there.
questions.learningObjective: explain why an idle processor under load points the search elsewhere

answer.exemplar: A boundary is a constraint placed on a quantity, and a quantity that has been shown to work at one size and fail at another is a quantity something is being measured against. The useful part is the gap between the two, because it names the range in which the constraint must lie, and a range is exactly what you want when you have not yet decided where to look. The critical companion measurement is the one that shows the total is not itself the problem: if the same content arrives when it is split into several exchanges, then whatever is refusing it is sensitive to the size of a single exchange rather than to the amount of work, which moves the search away from the application and towards the path and the peers at each end. What the boundary cannot do is name the component or give an exact figure, because only two points were tried and neither of them looked inside the exchange. The two most tempting overreaches are to take the failing size as a configured value and to take the silence as a refusal, and both turn a useful range into a confident wrong answer that sends the next hour of work to the wrong component.

questions.explanation: A working and a failing size bracket a constraint without naming it, and showing that the same content succeeds when split proves the total is not the issue, so the constraint applies to one exchange rather than to the work.
questions.hint: Ask what the two sizes bracket, and what the successful split rules out.
questions.learningObjective: explain what a size boundary brackets and what it cannot name
